# Raise the value and keep the price

Hormozi's main point in *$100M Offers* is that cutting your price is the commodity trap. When buyers see offers as interchangeable, they choose on price, and margins shrink until you're [working more for less](https://contentkungfu.beehiiv.com/p/alex-hormozi-100-million-offers-book-review). The way out is an offer that buyers [can't compare with anything else](https://www.supersummary.com/100m-offers/section-2-summary/), so they judge it on value instead of price.

## What to do: shorten the wait and remove the work

He measures value with the **Value Equation**:

> **Value = (Dream Outcome × Perceived Likelihood) ÷ (Time Delay × Effort & Sacrifice)**

The top two terms add value and the bottom two take it away ([summary](https://www.supersummary.com/100m-offers/section-3-summary/), [breakdown](https://creatoreconomy.so/p/the-value-equation-for-irresistible-products)). I'd put your effort into the bottom half. Most competitors already promise a big result. Very few make the result arrive faster or with less work. One summary quotes him saying that if you can cut the time to value to zero, the product becomes [infinitely valuable](https://publish.obsidian.md/charllaubscher/05+Love+%2B+Money/03+Process/Processes+for+Partnerships/Sales/The+Value+Equation). If the full result takes a long time, give buyers [short-term wins](https://bookbaseapp.substack.com/p/the-value-equation) early.

## How to build it: list every problem, then solve each one

1. **Write down every obstacle** your customer runs into before, during and after buying, in the order they hit them. The more problems you find, the more valuable the offer can be ([guide](https://www.claudepluginhub.com/skills/zacker-tech-hormozi/grand-slam-offer)).
2. **Turn each problem into a "How to…" solution.** "Healthy food is expensive" becomes "How to eat healthy for less than your current grocery bill" ([example](https://thepromptwarrior.beehiiv.com/p/let-alex-hormozi-transform-offer-money-printing-machine)).
3. **Pick a way to deliver each solution**: done-for-you, a template or a checklist. Then cut the ones that cost you a lot but matter little to the customer, and bundle the strong ones.
4. **Raise the perceived odds of success** with proof such as testimonials, results and a track record ([source](https://mikalangmann.beehiiv.com/p/alex-hormozi-creates-irresistible-offers-7eb5)).
5. **Add the extras around the offer**: a guarantee, bonuses that solve the next problem, real scarcity or urgency (limits that are actually true work better than discounts), and a name your customer relates to ([summary](https://www.supersummary.com/100m-offers/section-5-summary/)).

**What he would say:** don't cut the price. Find the slowest, most painful part of getting your result, then do it for the customer or make it happen faster. Keep adding solutions until the offer is worth far more than you charge, and then consider raising the price.

## Verdict: Yes, put the weakness in the ad. Say it first, then say "but" and follow it with your strongest true claim.

Hormozi calls this a **"damaging admission"** and says it's "probably my single favorite technique to use in persuasion." His reasoning is that the hardest part of marketing is getting people to believe you. If you name your flaws yourself, people can't hold them against you, and the claim that follows becomes more believable. In his words: "the more negatives I can say in the beginning, the more believable the thing that I say right afterwards is."

### How to word it

**1. Put the negative before "but" and the payoff after it.** He says "everything that is before the word but is diminished" and "everything that happens here after the word but is amplified." The order matters. "We're the best, but we're pricey" leaves the price ringing in their ears. "We're pricey, but you'll make it back in a month" leaves the payoff.

**2. Make the admission real and specific, even a little painful.** He says the "more true they are and the more damaging they are, the more believable" the claim that follows. One of his own examples sounds almost like a warning: *"You're going to have to go through hundreds of hours of videos. You're going to have to take five hours a day… but you're going to make more money than you've ever made in your life."* A fake flaw like "we care too much" doesn't work.

**3. Pick a flaw that sits next to the benefit.** His examples:
- Viagra's warning about an erection lasting more than four hours "amplified the power of the product."
- A 4.7-star rating from 3,000 reviews beats 5 stars from 19, because "the reviews that are negative give credence to the things that are positive."

The best flaw to admit is a side effect of the thing you're good at.

### Templates
- **"[Honest cost or effort], but [the result they want]."**
  "This isn't cheap and it takes 30 minutes a day, but in 90 days you'll have [result]."
- **"We're not [thing you're bad at]. We only [thing you're great at]."**
  "We're not the fastest. We're the ones who get it right the first time."
- **"Don't buy this if [who it's not for]. If you [who it is for], it'll [result]."**
  This also calls out the right audience, which he stresses separately.

### What to do next
Write down the top 2–3 objections prospects raise right now. Turn the most common one into the opener of your ad, put "but" after it, and finish with your strongest proof. Then test it against your current ad. Testing everything is the core of his *$100M Leads* approach.

Write your ads at a **3rd-grade reading level**, and never go above 5th. Your customers being educated doesn't change that. Hormozi doesn't make an exception for smart audiences, and his reasoning explains why he wouldn't.

**What he has said:**

- **The ad-copy rule is 3rd grade.** In his "12 Advertising Hacks" episode, he lists writing at a third-grade level as a way to remove friction. He says: *"Third grade level writing is accessible to pretty much everyone who can read,"* and *"Writing at a higher level, like ninth grade or a college level just puts up barriers you exclude people."* A summary of his July 2025 episode, "12 Persuasion Hacks I Use to Sell Anything," lists the same rule.
- **Simple is not dumb.** In his interview with Matt Gray he says: *"If you can write to a fifth grader… everyone else will understand,"* and *"People mistake making things simpler for making them dumber."* His editing rule while writing his books was: *"how can I make this simpler? How can I make this shorter? How can I make this easier?"*
- **Why it works on smart readers too:** he says to simplify sentences and words *"so that mental capacity is used on understanding the concepts."* An educated business owner scrolling past your ad has no more spare attention than anyone else. A community summary of another of his videos says he argues that simple language actually sounds smart.
- **His range:** in "9 Tips On Writing" he lists 3rd–5th grade vocabulary as one of the tips.

**What I'd do, the way he would:** Run every ad through the Hemingway App, which Hormozi fans commonly use to check grade level. Cut until it scores 3rd–5th grade. Use short sentences and active voice, and drop the adverbs. Your audience's intelligence should show up in the **substance**: specific numbers, real proof, an offer that's clearly better than the alternatives. Don't show it through long words. If you think your crowd is different, run the same offer at grade 3 and at grade 10 and let the results decide. That's how he'd settle it.

**Caveats:** I couldn't find a quote where he talks about educated audiences specifically. That part is my inference from his "simpler ≠ dumber" principle. No, don't start two or three new approaches. Based on what Hormozi has actually said, he'd tell you to put everything into the push you already started: run more of it and make it work better. You'd add one new channel only after you've hit the limit of this one. One month without hires isn't a sign the strategy failed. It's usually a sign it hasn't had enough volume or time.

**What he's said that applies:**

1. **Fix how you're running the plan before you change it.** In episode 863, "Stop Switching Strategies and Start Scaling," he says "many people want to change their plan rather than improve the execution of the plan they're currently on" and "we need perfect conviction about our plan more than we need a perfect plan." He also warns that "it's actually a lot longer to keep switching paths." He uses himself as the example: he was CEO of nine businesses and "wasn't making any money" because "I couldn't focus on any of them enough."

2. **The order is More → Better → New.** In the "Core Four on Steroids" chapter of *$100M Leads*, he says to "crank up the volume to max capacity" and "exhaust more better first." He also says "only once you've exhausted more better do the real returns come from doing new." He adds new channels one at a time ("just pick one, then max it out"), not two or three at once.

3. **A month is too soon to judge.** In the same episode 863 he says "if you're willing to suck at something for 100 days in a row, then you can beat most people at most things," and that "most of your competition quits after the first sign of difficulty." You're about 30 days into a 100-day standard.

4. **Pick the one lever that matters most.** In episode 794 (as summarized by Shortform) he says to find the single change that would transform the business and put all your resources on it, instead of spreading effort across a list of smaller tasks.

**What to do this week:**
- **Find where candidates drop off.** Count reach → applicants → interviews → offers → accepts.
- **If few people are applying, it's a volume problem.** Push volume much higher on the channel you're already using. His "Rule of 100" means 100 outreaches a day or at least $100 a day in ads.
- **If people apply but you're not hiring them, it's an execution problem.** Improve the job offer itself (pay, schedule, career path), respond faster, and tighten your interview process. Adding channels won't help here.
- **Set a date to decide.** Check again around day 90 to 100. Add one new channel only if this one is at full capacity and still isn't producing hires.

**Target under 10% monthly churn. Start worrying when it goes above 20%, and treat 30% or more as an emergency.** From what I found, Hormozi would tell you to fix churn before you spend another dollar on getting new members.

## The benchmarks he gives (from Skool's own data)

In a video on keeping customers, Hormozi gives these numbers for paid communities on Skool:

| Monthly churn | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Under 10%** | The best groups ("90% retention month over month") |
| **About 20%** | The platform average (80% retention) |
| **30% or more** | The "not good" groups. If you're here, he says "you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else." |

**When to worry, and when not to:** He says churn is naturally high in months 1–3 ("20% plus"). It drops to about 10% or less once members pass day 90, and to about 2% by month six. His warning: *"don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks"*, unless "basically everyone's leaving." So look at churn by cohort (members grouped by the month they joined). High churn in month one is normal. High churn after day 90 is the real problem.

## Why it matters: churn sets your ceiling

In Episode 340 of *The Game*, he breaks down a business with 13% monthly churn and $1,000/month pricing:
- **Lifetime value = price ÷ churn**, so $1,000 ÷ 13% ≈ $7,700.
- **Max size ≈ lifetime value × new sales per month**. At 100 sales a month, the business levels off around $770K/month no matter how much more it sells.
- If churn falls to 3%, lifetime value goes to about $33K and the ceiling rises more than fourfold. In his words, churn "is going to start eating a bigger and bigger percentage of the new business that is coming in."

So if your community stops growing even though new members keep joining, churn is the cause, not marketing.

## What he'd have you do, in order
1. **Fix the first month.** Pin one quick win members can get "ideally within the first 24 hours." Set accurate expectations when you sell, and show up every day. He says owners who were active daily had "significantly higher retention."
2. **Tag every cancellation reason** (price, overwhelm, not using it, not what they expected). After every ~20 cancellations, fix the top one or two reasons. Don't react to any single complaint.
3. **Cut friction instead of adding content.** He calls overwhelm "the number one reason people churn, outside of price."
4. **Get them to belong.** Introduce each new member to about 10 regulars. By month six, people stay because of the other members.
5. **Offer an annual plan** at roughly a 16–17% discount. He says "annual always has lower churn than monthly."
6. **Keep the bar to join high and the price low.** A Skool Games recap says that combination lowers churn, while a high price with low entry standards hurts retention.

**If I were you:** work out your churn by cohort this week. If members who've been in for 90+ days still churn above 10%, stop scaling ads and spend the next month on the first two steps.

**Take the percentage of revenue.** That's my recommendation, and it's how Hormozi's own deal-making points.

One caveat up front: I couldn't find Hormozi ever saying "always take revenue over profit." His public comments on this are scattered. So the recommendation is built from what he has said and done, not from one quote.

**What he's said and done**

- **His early Acquisition.com deals had both options.** On the *How I Invest* podcast he said: "we had an element of cash flow, which is either a profit share or a revenue share, depending on how volatile the business was." He didn't take profit share by default. He picked based on how much the number could swing. He gave a reason too: "we need cash flow because we have a huge team helping you put all these things together." Your consulting time is the same: you're doing work now and need to get paid now.
- **He insists on control when his pay depends on the client's numbers.** Same interview: "We look for a lot of majority covenants even if we're not in a majority position… we wanna have a good amount of operating control." Later he started putting his own cash into companies because it made things "less like we're consultants for hire." Profit share only works when you control or can audit the expenses.
- **He worries about whether the client reports honestly.** On a call-in episode about performance pricing, he asked what systems make sure clients are honest when billing depends on their results. He said this pricing works best with clients who clearly have the money ("whales") and when there are controls to catch abuse.
- **A summary of a 2026 interview says he thinks rev share has "attribution problems."** That means it's hard to prove your work caused the revenue. If you take rev share, define the baseline and how it's measured up front.

**Why that points to revenue**

You're a consultant, not an owner with control rights. Profit sits below every decision you don't control: the owner's salary, new hires, software, a new car "for the business," moving costs between years. Revenue is a single figure that's hard to fudge and easy to check against bank deposits. Profit can be pushed to zero without anyone technically lying.

His line about prioritizing profit over revenue is advice for running your own business. It's not about how a consultant should get paid.

**How to set it up, Hormozi-style**

1. Ask for a percentage of revenue above an agreed baseline. That mirrors his "30% of everything above that" structure and fixes the attribution problem.
2. Get some cash up front or a small retainer so you're paid for the work while you do it.
3. Put audit or reporting rights in the contract: monthly statements plus access to the payment processor or bank data.

**When profit share could make sense:** you have real control over spending (a vote or covenants on budget and hires), you get full access to the books, and the profit percentage is several times bigger than the revenue offer. That's the only setup where Hormozi takes profit-based cash flow. Without those, you'd be taking on an owner's risk without an owner's control.

Bootstrap. Get your customers to pay for your growth, not investors. As far as I could find, that's what Hormozi would tell you, and it's how he built his own companies.

**What he says and did**

- **His record.** His bios say his first business was a gym he opened in 2013 and grew to six locations in about three years. He then scaled three more companies to over $120M in combined sales without outside capital ([WWD](https://wwd.com/business-news/business-features/alex-hormozi-business-journey-1235367351), [Flaunt](https://flaunt.com/post/alex-hormozi)). On his podcast he describes building "with 100% equity without taking on outside capital or investors" and says "I took no outside money to do that" ([The Game, Ep 346 transcript](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/how-to-make-a-profit-in-30-days-with-a-credit-card-ep-346)).
- **His method is customer-financed acquisition.** He doesn't use investors' money to pay for growth: "get your customers to pay for all of your marketing and your acquisition costs" and "I'm using my customer's money to finance all of the growth in this business" ([Ep 346](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/how-to-make-a-profit-in-30-days-with-a-credit-card-ep-346)). In *$100M Money Models* the target is to earn back more than twice your customer acquisition cost plus delivery cost in gross profit within 30 days of getting a customer. If you hit that, cash stops limiting your growth ([SuperSummary](https://www.supersummary.com/100m-money-models/summary/), [Shortform](https://shortform.com/podcast/episode/the-game-w-alex-hormozi-2025-11-14-episode-summary-13-levels-of-customer-financed-acquisition-100m-lost-chapters-audiobook)).
- **He addresses your question directly.** A summary of his video "The 4 Proven Ways To Build Wealth In 2026" says bootstrapping is "usually best for first-time founders," while raising capital "fits large capital-intensive opportunities" ([Rosetta](https://rosetta.to/u/alexhormozi/2026)). That's the page's paraphrase, not his exact words.

**Why bootstrapping is the right call for a first business**

When you start your first business, you don't yet know how to sell. Raising money lets you skip learning that. You give up equity to cover the cost of not knowing how to sell, then you spend the money on ads and staff that don't work. If you have to make the business profitable from customer number one, you're forced to fix the offer, the pricing and the sales process, and those are the skills that build wealth. You also keep 100% of the company.

**What to do**

1. Pick something you can start selling in weeks, like a service, an agency or local business work, so you don't need money up front to build a product.
2. Price it high enough that the first sale pays back what it cost to get that customer, and aim for 2x within 30 days.
3. Reinvest that profit into getting more customers. Once you're profitable, you can raise money later from a position of strength if you ever need to.

**The one exception:** if your idea can't make money until a lot of capital goes in first, like hardware, biotech or a heavily regulated business, Hormozi's own framework says to raise. For most first businesses, though, needing investors means you should pick a different business model, not go find investors.

Hormozi's answer would be to spend the first, protected block of every day on whatever brings in money, which for you almost certainly means getting more leads. Everything else waits until the afternoon.

**The schedule I'd pick for you, based on what he's said:**

1. **Plan tomorrow tonight.** Before bed, write down the one money-making goal for the next day. He plans his next day the night before so he never wakes up wondering what to do ([summary of his routine](https://whysaksham.beehiiv.com/p/the-daily-schedule-that-made-me-10x-more-productive)).
2. **No meetings until noon, and the morning goes to revenue.** He keeps about 6am to noon blocked on his calendar with no meetings. His rule for what goes in that block: "Do the ones that make you the most money first." He also keeps the same wake time on weekdays and weekends, and he has no morning routine to speak of. He has coffee with his wife and starts working ([The Game, ep. 549](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/the-surprising-productivity-hacks-you-have-to-try-ep-549)).
3. **Fill that block with the "Rule of 100."** In *$100M Leads* he says to do 100 marketing actions a day for 100 days in a row. That could be 100 outreach messages, 100 minutes of content, or $100 on ads. Pick one lead source (warm outreach, cold outreach, content or paid ads), get good at it, and only then add another. If you're starting with warm outreach, go through everyone you know, about 100 people a day, and move on from anyone who hasn't replied after 2–3 tries ([Shortform summary](https://www.shortform.com/blog/?p=146297), [Medium](https://medium.com/@zack_liu/the-rule-of-100-is-the-only-productivity-metric-that-matters-26f1504ee4a8)).
4. **Use the afternoon for managing.** Sales calls, delivering for clients, email and admin go here. He separates "maker" time, meaning long uninterrupted blocks, from "manager" time, meaning short slots and meetings. **Raise your prices. Don't hold them to protect the close rate.** Hormozi has already answered this for a business with your exact numbers.

It's an HVAC duct-cleaning company doing about $1.2M with a 38% net margin ($479K profit) and an 82% close rate on in-home inspections. Average ticket was $1,575 per unit.

**What he said:**
- On the close rate: *"Whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale."* An 82% close rate means you're underpriced.
- His recommendation: raise prices **10%, to about $1,650 per unit.** *"As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money."*
- The payoff: *"That 10% price raise for you equals roughly a 25% increase in net profit."* At that volume, that's roughly $100K+ a year.
- Why it may not hurt the close rate: for ordinary service businesses, a higher price can make customers more confident the company will deliver. In his value equation, that's "perceived likelihood of achievement." He also pointed to the "virtuous cycle of pricing" from *$100M Offers*: higher prices bring better customers who are more invested.
- The owner had already raised prices 23% after an earlier workshop. Their close rate went **up**, and so did revenue.

**The math holds up.** At a 38% margin, each job leaves you 38% of the price. After a 10% raise it leaves about 48%. 0.38 / 0.48 ≈ 0.79, and 0.79 × 82% ≈ 65%. So your close rate has to drop by about 17 points before you're worse off. If a lot of your costs are fixed rather than per-job, that floor moves up a little, to roughly 66–68%, which still leaves plenty of room.

**What to do:** Quote $1,650 per unit on new inspections starting now. Track the close rate over the next 30–60 days. If it stays above about 65%, keep the price, and then test another increase, since he sees anything near 80% as a sign there's still room. Only roll back if it falls below that line.

**Why he'd say yes**

- **Most of the profit comes from the premium tier.** In Ep 986 of his podcast *The Game*, he runs the numbers: a $100 product sold to 90 people brings in $9,000, or about $3,600 profit at a 40% margin. A $1,000 offer bought by just 10 of them brings in $10,000. Delivering it costs little extra, so nearly all of that is profit, and the premium tier ends up producing about three-quarters of total profit. His reasoning is that if you make an offer 10x more expensive, the chance someone buys it is greater than zero, and that alone pays. The danger he does name is the middle of the market: "The middle is where people die."
- **Price it 5–10x higher, not a bit higher.** A summary of Ep 996 attributes this to him: "every new tier of pricing should increase significantly (5 to 10 times)." He builds on the idea that a small share of customers produces most of the profit. For you, that means roughly $500–$1,000/month. Something like $150 is too close to the core price to be worth it.
- **The cheaper tier and the expensive tier help each other.** On a throwback upsell episode (Ep 378, re-aired as Ep 895), he reviewed a creator who had a cheaper membership and a high-ticket offer side by side. His verdict: "that probably anchors really well." The membership brings in the people the premium tier is sold to, and the premium tier makes $100 look cheap.

**About the distraction worry**

I didn't find him warning that a premium tier distracts from the core product. His warnings about focus are about adding new products and new kinds of customers before the first offer works at scale. A premium tier for your existing members isn't that. It's the same customers and the same problem, with more access and faster results. Two cautions he does give:

- Limit premium one-on-one work to about 5–10% of your time (Ep 986).
- From a Skool Games session (Skool is the community platform he co-owns): high prices with loose entry requirements lead to poor retention. Make the premium tier something members apply for, not a button anyone can click.

**What I'd do in his style**

1. Ask his question: "If I charged 10x, what would I include?"
2. Pick the parts that members value a lot but cost you little to deliver: small-group hot seats, reviews of members' offers and pitches, direct access to you, and done-for-you templates.
3. Offer it only to current members, by application, at about $750–$1,000/month.
4. Leave the $100 community as it is. Expect maybe 5–10% of members to move up.

The one case where I'd hold off: if the $100 community is losing members quickly, fix that first.

It isn't a sign to change channels.

2. **His order is More, then Better, then New.** "More" (volume) comes first. "New" (new channels and tactics) comes only after More and Better stop working, because new things cost you for certain and pay off only maybe. His slogan for this is "volume negates luck." Most plateaus come from too few new ad creatives, since each ad wears out. Summaries of his talks say he builes around 80% of new ads from proven winners and 20% from new ideas, then makes about 10 variations of each winner.

3. **Expand audiences first, then platforms.** From the roadmap: *"First, you expand new audiences on your best platform."* Only *"after your team can get consistent results"* do you *"add another platform."* Going bigger on Meta means reaching people who know less about you. Your ads will need to educate more. Your current ads were probably built for the warmest buyers.

4. **Raise what each customer is worth so you can pay more per customer.** He says *"the business that can make more money from its customer than its competitors wins"* and *"I can pay more to get them."* He also says to spend *"as much as you possibly can and then wait until something else in your business breaks."* For an info product, that means adding upsells and continuity offers (e.g. memberships) on the back end. Then a higher cost per customer is still profitable and the $100k wall moves.

5. **You're below his size threshold for adding channels.** A summary of his "Advertise More" episode (Ep 734) says to stay on one channel, one avatar and one product until about $1M/month before adding secondary channels. At $500k/month, you aren't there yet. That figure comes from a secondhand summary, so treat it as rough.

- **Add affiliates, but recruit them through Meta.** He wrote: *"I expanded my paid ads to include potential affiliates and this paved the way for my affiliate programs."* In his framework, affiliates are a later step on top of a working channel, not a replacement for it.

If people pay for ten things and use one, *"you feel like you're only getting 20% of the value."*
- **Cutting worked.** He describes a Skool community that deleted content, and its monthly churn reportedly fell **from 30% to 5%**. Its starting point was the same as yours.
- **Benchmarks:** the Skool average is 80% monthly retention, and the best groups keep 90% or more. At 30% churn you're well below average.
- **Price:** if your *ideal* customers say it's too expensive, *"you can add a lower tier."* If non-ideal people say it, *"just ignore it,"* because the price is doing its job as a filter. He gives Skool's own move as an example: it added a $9 tier under the $99 plan.

## What to do instead

1. **Survey current and cancelling members.** Ask what one thing they would fight to keep if everything else were deleted, and what they wouldn't miss. Look for patterns rather than reacting to single answers.
2. **Cut down to the top one or two things.** Give busy members a simple weekly rhythm, for example one live call with a recording and one "best of" post. Keep the extra depth optional. He calls this thinking in "value per second."
3. **Fix the first month**, which is where most churn happens. Pin a quick win so new members get value within about 24 hours.
4. **Check who says "too expensive."** If they're your ideal customers, add a cheaper, smaller tier. If not, ignore it.

The value-equation framing from *$100M Offers* points the same way: **lowering effort and sacrifice** raises perceived value. Your "can't keep up" cancellations show the effort is already too high, and more trainings and calls would add to it.

- His 33% floor matches the tax rule that makes this tax-free. Under Section 1042, you can defer capital gains only if the company is a C-corp, the ESOP owns at least 30% after the sale, and you reinvest the money in qualifying securities. An S-corp or LLC doesn't get this as-is.
- I couldn't find anywhere he talks about selling 100% to employees. The 33–49% advice is from one short segment where he compares exit options.

Talk to an ESOP attorney and a valuation firm before you set this up.
